args.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Census Records to Trace Family

United States federal census records are among the most important genealogical sources. A census was taken every ten years beginning in 1790. FamilySearch has a census collection with an index and images for each federal census year from 1790 through 1950. Most of these censuses are also on subscription sites such as Ancestry, Findmypast, and MyHeritage, which require a paid subscription for full access. To search census records on FamilySearch.org, click Search, then Records, enter your ancestor's name, and filter by record type "Census, Voter Lists."

What a census recorded about each household member changed over time. From 1790 through 1840, only the head of household is named, and everyone else is counted only as tally marks within age and sex categories. From 1850 through 1870, every free person in the household is listed by name with age, sex, and birthplace, but relationship to the head of household is not stated. Beginning in 1880, every person is listed by name together with their relationship to the head of household.

By tracing a family through multiple census years, you can watch children grow up, track a family's migration, and identify previously unknown relatives. Each census decade can point you to a new location or a maiden name. When searching, try alternate spellings of surnames and consider that ages reported in different census years may vary by several years.

## Sources

- [United States Census — Background](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census#Background)
- [United States Census — Strategy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census#Strategy)

args.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Irish Church Records

Church records are among the most important sources for Irish genealogy research. The two main denominations that kept parish registers in Ireland were the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of Ireland (Anglican). Roman Catholic registers generally begin in the early 1800s, while Church of Ireland registers often start earlier, in the 1700s. Many original registers were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire, but microfilmed copies and transcriptions survive. FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a large collection of Irish Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers, which are freely searchable at FamilySearch.org.

To find Irish church records on FamilySearch, go to FamilySearch.org and click Search, then Records. Enter your ancestor's name and select Ireland as the country. Filter results by record type to narrow to church records including baptisms, marriages, and burials. The National Library of Ireland also holds a large collection of Catholic parish registers on microfilm, many of which have been digitized and are available online. The Representative Church Body Library in Dublin holds Church of Ireland registers not destroyed in 1922.

Irish church records typically contain baptism (christening) records listing the child's name, baptism date, parents' names, and sometimes the townland or parish of residence. Marriage records list the names of the bride and groom, the date and place of marriage, and witnesses. Burial records list the name of the deceased and the burial date. Earlier records may contain less detail. Some registers also include sponsor names for baptisms, which can help identify other family members.

## Sources

- [Ireland Church Records — Overview of Irish Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Overview_of_Irish_Church_Records)
- [Ireland Church Records — Finding Church Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Finding_Church_Records_on_FamilySearch)
- [Ireland Church Records — What Church Records Contain](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#What_Church_Records_Contain)

# FamilySearch Wiki: Death Records, 1800s

Death records before civil registration was established are harder to find. In the United States, statewide death registration typically began between 1880 and 1920 depending on the state. For deaths in the mid-to-late 1800s, researchers should check death certificates (where available), church burial registers, cemetery records, obituaries in local newspapers, and probate records. Because statewide registration often came late, pre-registration deaths may only appear in county or municipal records, and survival is uneven. Pennsylvania, for example, began statewide civil registration of deaths in 1906; before that, death records are found at the county or municipal level. When a death certificate does exist, information such as a decedent's parentage was supplied by an informant named on the certificate, who may not have had firsthand knowledge of that prior generation — meaning parentage stated on a death certificate is secondary evidence and is strongest when corroborated by other sources.

# FamilySearch Wiki: Italian Birth Records

Civil registration (Stato Civile) of births, marriages, and deaths began in most of Italy in 1809 under Napoleonic rule, lapsed in many regions after 1815, and resumed nationwide in 1866 following unification. Civil birth records (atti di nascita) are the single most useful source for Italian genealogy after 1866. They record the child's name, the date and place of birth, and the names, ages, occupations, and residence of both parents.

Before civil registration, and as a parallel source afterward, Catholic parish registers (registri parrocchiali) recorded baptisms. A baptismal record (atto di battesimo) usually gives the baptism date, the child's name, the parents' names, and the godparents. Parish registers in many Italian dioceses begin in the late 1500s following the Council of Trent.

Many Italian civil registration records have been digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog, searchable by the comune (town) where the event occurred. Records less than 100 years old are generally restricted by Italian privacy law and must be requested directly from the local Ufficio dello Stato Civile.

Here's what the FamilySearch Wiki guidance covers for finding German church records:

---

## Finding German Church Records for Your Ancestors

### What German Church Records Contain
German church records (Kirchenbücher) are among the most important genealogical sources for German ancestors and typically include:
- **Baptismal/christening registers** — name, date, parents, godparents
- **Marriage registers** — names of bride and groom, witnesses, parents
- **Burial/death registers** — name, date, age, sometimes cause of death

These records often predate civil registration (which began in most German states around 1874–1876), sometimes going back to the 1500s–1600s.

---

### Key Steps to Find the Right Records

1. **Identify the ancestral parish.** Church records are organized by parish, not by civil jurisdiction. You need to know the village your ancestor came from, then determine which church parish it belonged to. A **gazetteer** (Ortsverzeichnis) can help you identify the correct parish for a given village.

2. **Search the FamilySearch Catalog.** Go to [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/catalog/search) and search by **place** (the German village or parish name). This will show what records have been microfilmed or digitized.

3. **Check Archion and Matricula.** Two major sites host digitized German Protestant and Catholic church records:
   - **[Archion](https://www.archion.de)** — digitized Lutheran/Protestant church books
   - **[Matricula](https://data.matricula-online.eu)** — digitized Catholic church books

4. **Use FamilySearch Collections.** Many German church records are indexed and searchable directly on FamilySearch under Germany collections.

---

### Tips
- Germany's religious landscape matters: most of northern Germany is **Lutheran (Protestant)**, while southern Germany (Bavaria, etc.) is largely **Catholic**. Knowing your ancestor's religion helps narrow the archive.
- If records aren't on FamilySearch or Archion/Matricula, the originals are typically held in **regional church archives** (Landeskirchliches Archiv for Protestant records, diocesan archives for Catholic records).

The guidance has been saved to your research log for future reference. Would you like to search for records for a specific German village or parish?

Protestant (Evangelisch) and Catholic (Katholisch) parishes recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials, with many registers beginning in the 1600s and some Catholic registers reaching back to the mid-1500s. Each register is kept by the parish, not by the town, so identifying the correct parish is the essential first step.

To find the parish that served an ancestor's village, use a gazetteer. Meyers Orts- und Verkehrs-Lexikon des Deutschen Reichs lists every place in the 1871-1918 German Empire and identifies the civil registration office and the Protestant and Catholic parishes serving it.

Many German church records have been microfilmed or digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog under the parish or town name. Others remain only at the parish, the regional church archive (Landeskirchliches Archiv or Kirchenbuchamt), or on subscription sites such as Archion (Protestant) and Matricula (Catholic).

Marriage records in the United States were typically kept by county clerks, churches, or state vital records offices depending on the time period and location. Civil War military records are held primarily at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. args.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Probate or Will Records

Probate records are created when a deceased person's estate is settled through a court process. They include wills, inventories of property, letters of administration, and final settlements. Probate records can identify family members (especially heirs), provide an economic snapshot, and confirm dates and places. In the United States, probate is handled at the county level, and records are held by county probate courts or surrogate courts. FamilySearch has indexed and digitized probate records from many counties across the country.

To find probate records on FamilySearch, search the FamilySearch Catalog by state and county under the "Probate records" category. Many collections are browse-only images. When a will is found, it should be read carefully — testators often name children, grandchildren, and in-laws by name. Intestate records (for those who died without a will) list heirs and their relationships to the deceased, which can be equally valuable for establishing family connections.

## Sources

- [United States Probate Records — What Are Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Probate_Records#What_Are_Probate_Records)
- [United States Probate Records — Finding Probate Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Probate_Records#Finding_Probate_Records_on_FamilySearch)
